newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kohl wishes Yeltsin "all the best" for surgery.
newsitem.headline: Kohl wishes Yeltsin "all the best" for surgery.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl made a brief stopover in Moscow on Saturday for talks with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and passed on his good wishes to President Boris Yeltsin for his forthcoming heart surgery.

"In these coming days we wish Boris Yeltsin all the best," Kohl told journalists after meeting Chernomyrdin for an hour at Moscow's snowswept Vnukovo airport while his plane refuelled on the way home from Japan after an Asian tour.
Kohl has closer ties with Yeltsin than any other Western leader and last saw him in September in Moscow.

"I hope the president will return (to work) soon and refreshed," Kohl said. He indicated no major decision on NATO enlargement -- a sore point for Moscow -- would be taken until the Russian president was back in action.

Chernomyrdin, who will stand in for Yeltsin during the operation, received personal praise from Kohl, who said: "These are by no means easy times and it is important that you are here to act with a sense of duty and responsibility."

The health of the 65-year-old president has worried Western leaders who regard him as the guarantor of reforms and stability in Russia. Chernomyrdin is seen in the West as the best guarantee of stability in Russia in Yeltsin's absence.
"All preparations for the operation have been completed but the decision has to be taken by the doctors," Chernomyrdin said after the hour-long meeting.

Russian surgeons have not announced a date for the multiple bypass operation to improve the supply of blood to Yeltsin's heart, but Chernomyrdin's remarks reinforced the impression that the date was not far away.
The Russian daily newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda said it would be on Wednesday but gave no source for its report.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told Ekho Moskvy radio on Saturday the operation, led by Russian surgeon Renat Akchurin, would last between six and eight hours in the Cardiological Centre on Moscow's western outskirts.
U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who will be a consultant to the Russian doctors, said in Houston on Friday that he expected the surgery to go ahead early next week.
DeBakey, who was due to arrive in Moscow on Sunday, said Yeltsin had been treated for anaemia and thyroid problems and that he appeared now to be ready for surgery.
"On the basis of what they have told me, it looks like we should be able to go ahead with the operation early next week. He's improved," he told Reuters.
DeBakey, 88, said he would meet Yeltsin's medical team on Monday for final consultations.
He examined Yeltsin in late September and predicted a full recovery for the president, but recommended that he rest for at least six weeks before the operation.

DeBakey has posted a special page on the Internet which could be updated during his visit. On Saturday it carried a statement that no information could currently be provided on Yeltsin's state of health.
Chernomyrdin has already taken on some of Yeltsin's duties and, if all goes according to plan, will assume his full powers for only a few hours.
If the president does not recover, the prime minister would take over for three months to prepare for an election.

Yeltsin's four-month absence from the Kremlin has prompted talk of a power struggle from which Chernomyrdin has sought to distance himself in public. There have been widespread allegations that Yeltsin's chief of staff Anatoly Chubais is wielding power as regent in the president's name.
But Kremlin spokesman Yastrzhembsky, in his radio interview, stressed that Yeltsin was personally studying and signing all the decrees issued over his signature.
